title: Accompanying the dying
hookLine: Tolstoy's Ivan Ilyich: the family keeps up a polite lie, and a young servant simply stays
tomorrow: why would a man plant a tree he'll never eat from?

cards: A chair beside a bed, and a visitor who has no idea what to say, so they talk about parking and the weather. Tolstoy wrote a whole story about that room.
In The Death of Ivan Ilyich, a judge is dying, and everyone around him, his wife, his daughter, the doctors, keeps up a polite lie: he's only ill, and with treatment he'll get better.
Ivan knows it isn't true, and the lie torments him more than the pain. Only one person in the house won't tell it. Gerasim, a young peasant who serves in the house.

teach.h: HE HOLDS IVAN'S LEGS ALL NIGHT.
teach.b: Gerasim sits up through the night holding Ivan's legs on his shoulders, because that eases him.

When Ivan apologizes for the trouble, Gerasim answers, more or less: we'll all die someday, so why shouldn't I take a little trouble? Ivan is at ease only with him. So here's the debate, and both sides are real.

teach.h: THE FAMILY: HOPE, DON'T SAY DYING.
teach.b: The family's side: don't say dying. Hope carries people. Naming death can sound like giving up, and some who are dying don't want to hear it.
That isn't cruelty. It's love that's afraid.
Gerasim's side: don't pretend. When someone stays and doesn't perform, the dying person can stop performing too.
Tolstoy tells it so the lie isolates Ivan and the honesty comforts him, and the one who knows how is the plainest person in the house. There's a plain word for what Gerasim does: presence.
Tend the pain, don't lie, and stay.
It doesn't take the right words.

how: Readers of Tolstoy's story, and some who sit with the dying, take Gerasim as a model: tend the body, don't keep up a pretense, and stay, with few words.

o: staying beside someone near death, honestly and gently
the hospital paperwork done near the end of a life
the prayers a priest says at the bedside of the dying

games.q: who did what in Ivan's house: tap the pairs.
p: a dying judge, worn out by the lie
a servant who stayed and didn't pretend
kept up the polite lie, out of fear
staying, honestly, with nothing to fix

s: in Tolstoy's story, the doctors comfort Ivan most
the doctors keep up the polite lie. the comfort comes from Gerasim, a servant.
Gerasim says we'll all die someday, so why not take a little trouble
that's his answer when Ivan apologizes for the trouble he's causing.
helping the dying mostly means finding exactly the right words
the popular worry. Gerasim's gift is staying, honestly, with very few words.

games.q: your cousin says: never say 'dying' to someone who is dying; it takes their hope. what's the best case for her side?
o: hope can carry people, and some dying people don't want to hear it; her silence is love.
she's afraid of hospitals and wants a reason to skip the visits.
she doesn't know the person is dying, so she can't be blamed for it.
games.why: the family's side is love that's afraid, and it's real. Tolstoy's story weighs it against Gerasim's: honest, gentle, and staying.

practice: Sit the way you might beside a bed: feet down, hands open in your lap, nothing to fix. For the rest of the sit, practice only what Gerasim did, which is stay. When a thought says find something to say, let it go by, and stay.

wordCard.voice: Accompanying the dying: staying beside someone at the end, without the polite lie and without leaving. Gerasim's way.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: presence, the gift the servant had and the doctors didn't. Five of seven.

sources.ref: Leo Tolstoy, The Death of Ivan Ilyich, chapters 7-8 (the lie; Gerasim holding Ivan's legs; 'we shall all die')
